title: Protestants distinguish justification from sanctification; Chamier on word swap
source_text: XXII. Inde est quod hominis justificationem distinguunt ab illius regeneratione, sive sanctificatione, quae docent esse duo beneficia, natura sua distincta, licet ab invicem separari non possint. Deus enim, ex illorum sententia, neminem a poena peccatorum absolvit, quin eum a peccati servitute liberet, & peccati sordes ab eo abstergat, ejusque animum nova justitia exornet, & vero ac syncero Dei amore perfundat & imbuat. Sed justificationis nomine solam absolutionem, per sanctificationem vero purgationem a peccati foeditate, & internae justitiae donationem significare solent. Quamvis hasce voces quandoque in Scriptura sacra permutari; ut observat Chamierus, tom. 3. lib. 10. cap. 5. num. 6. Non sum, inquit, tam inepti vocabulorum aestimatores, ut nesciamus, aut tam importuni Sophistae, ut nolimus justificationis sanctificationisque voces permutari; imo sanctos hac praecipue ratione scimus appellari, quod in Christo habeant remissionem peccatorum. Et legimus in Apocalypsi, Qui justus est justificetur adhuc, quod nisi de profectu inhaerentis justitiae, nequeat intelligi, & aliis forte locis non negamus promiscue venire in usum.
pass_a_gloss: Hence it is that they distinguish a man's justification from his regeneration or sanctification, which they teach to be two benefits, distinct by nature, although they cannot be separated from each other. For God, in their opinion, absolves no one from the penalty of sins without freeing him from the slavery of sin, wiping the filth of sin from him, adorning his mind with new righteousness, and pouring into him and imbuing him with a true and sincere love of God. But by the name of justification they are wont to signify only absolution, but by sanctification the cleansing from the foulness of sin and the gift of inward righteousness. Although these words are sometimes interchanged in sacred Scripture; as Chamier observes, tom. 3 lib. 10 cap. 5 n. 6. We are not, he says, such inept estimators of words that we do not know, or such importunate Sophists that we are unwilling, that the words of justification and sanctification be interchanged; nay, we know saints are called especially for this reason, that in Christ they have remission of sins. And we read in the Apocalypse, He that is just, let him be justified still, which unless of the progress of inherent righteousness cannot be understood, and in other places perhaps we do not deny they come into use promiscuously.
pass_b_english: Protestants distinguish justification (absolution) from sanctification (inward cleansing)—inseparable yet distinct.
Chamier allows occasional Scriptural word-swap; Rev 22:11 is inherent-progress sense.
